sentences: Dark clouds fill the sky, and a small village huddles beside frozen water.
This is Winter Landscape, by Jacob van Ruisdael, the great landscape painter of the Dutch Golden Age.
It was painted in oil on canvas around 1665, and it is a small picture, just 42 centimetres high and 49.7 centimetres wide.
It came to the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam in 1870, as part of a collector's bequest.
Look first at the sky.
Ominous dark clouds take up most of the canvas.
In the pictures of his Amsterdam years the sky often fills two-thirds of the canvas, and here the weather, more than the land, is the true subject.
Now look to the left.
A low, raking sunlight enters from the left and lights only parts of the snowy ground and the buildings.
The museum singles out this light.
Between the places it reaches and the places it does not, the depth of winter opens up.
Look at the village.
A square tower and a few houses stand along the frozen water, and on the left there is a farm barn.
In this small picture, the tower is the one strong vertical reaching up towards the sky.
Find the people on the ice.
A few figures are there with a sled.
They are warmly dressed, but as the museum observes, they seem insignificant in the face of this inclement weather.
Ruisdael painted around twenty-five winter landscapes.
On the ice of his contemporary Avercamp, crowds of skaters enjoy themselves, but the museum remarks that a cheerful crowd would have been out of place in a winter scene by Ruisdael.
It is the same frozen water, the same Dutch winter, in a completely different mood.
He was born in Haarlem in 1628 or 1629, into a family of painters.
His father, Isaack, was a frame-maker and art dealer, and his uncle Salomon was a well-known painter of river scenes.
His earliest known landscapes, signed and dated 1646, were made when he was still a teenager.
Around 1657 he moved to Amsterdam, a prosperous city with a bigger market for his work, and he lived and worked there for the rest of his life.
He died in 1682 and was buried in the church of Saint Bavo in his native Haarlem.
His signature, JVRuisdael, appears on this canvas.
Step back and look once more.
Into a picture hardly larger than a page, he has poured the whole weight of a winter sky, and the people below it seem to hold their breath.
On the coldest day of the year, take a moment to look up at the sky outside your window.
